721.event_title: Frederick Douglass delivers What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
721.place: Corinthian Hall, Rochester, New York, United States
721.event: At the invitation of the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society, Frederick Douglass addressed an audience of five to six hundred people, each paying a small admission fee, at Corinthian Hall on 5 July 1852. He praised the signers of the Declaration of Independence as great men and then set out how the freedoms celebrated on Independence Day were denied to enslaved Americans. The address became the most celebrated of his speeches.
721.explanation: Douglass understood exactly the audience before him, people proud of the nation's founding, and built his argument on their own reverence for its ideals.
721.tie_back: The kural says that those who know the full range of words and first take the measure of the assembly will not falter before it, and Douglass's speech is a model of reading an audience and speaking without faltering.
721._accuracy_note: A strong example of commanding an assembly with mastery of words; how deliberately he sized up this particular audience is inferred from the structure of the speech rather than documented.

722.event_title: David Hilbert presents his problems to the International Congress of Mathematicians
722.event: At the second International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris, David Hilbert gave a talk in which he described ten problems from a list of twenty-three unsolved questions he believed would shape mathematics in the coming century. The full list appeared in the published paper. Several of the problems became central to twentieth-century mathematics, and the organisers later placed his paper among the plenary lectures because of its importance.
722.explanation: Before an audience of the world's leading mathematicians, Hilbert set out his vision so clearly that it directed much of their research for generations.
722.tie_back: The kural says the most learned of the learned are those who can present their learning before the learned so that it truly reaches them, which is what Hilbert's address achieved.
722._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural: a master presenting ideas to his peers in a way that took hold of the whole field.

723.event_title: Margaret Chase Smith delivers her Declaration of Conscience
723.place: United States Senate, Washington, D.C., United States
723.event: Senator Margaret Chase Smith of Maine, then the only woman in the Senate and a first-term member of Senator Joseph McCarthy's own party, rose in the Senate chamber to deliver a fifteen-minute speech criticising the use of the Senate for unproved charges and character attacks. McCarthy sat two rows behind her, and on her way to the chamber he had reminded her of his influence over convention votes. Six Republican colleagues joined her Declaration of Conscience, and McCarthy later had her removed from the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.
723.explanation: At a time when many senators feared McCarthy, Smith chose to speak against him in front of the whole Senate and accepted the political cost.
723.tie_back: The kural says that those willing to face death among enemies are many, but those who stand fearless in an assembly are rare, and Smith's speech is a celebrated example of that rarer courage.
723._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of civil courage before an assembly, the kural's central contrast.

724.event_title: Andrew Wiles announces, then repairs, his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
724.place: Isaac Newton Institute, Cambridge, England, and Princeton, United States
724.event: At the end of a series of three lectures at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge on 23 June 1993, Andrew Wiles announced a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem. Later in 1993 a referee checking the details found a serious gap. Wiles worked for about a year with his former student Richard Taylor to correct it, and the completed proof, with a companion paper by Taylor and Wiles, was published in the Annals of Mathematics in 1995.
724.explanation: Wiles put his work before the most expert audience available, accepted the flaw their scrutiny revealed, and drew on a colleague's help to complete it.
724.tie_back: The kural asks the learned to set their knowledge before the learned and then take from others whatever lies beyond their own, which is the cycle Wiles went through between his 1993 lectures and the 1995 proof.
724._accuracy_note: Strong fit for presenting before peers and then learning from their scrutiny; the help came from a former student rather than a more learned senior, a small difference from the kural's wording.

725.event_title: Thurgood Marshall, trained at Howard, wins Brown v. Board of Education
725.place: Howard University Law School and the U.S. Supreme Court, Washington, D.C., United States
725.event: Thurgood Marshall graduated first in his class from Howard University Law School in 1933, where his mentor Charles Hamilton Houston encouraged students to use the law for social change. Marshall went on to argue thirty-two cases before the U.S. Supreme Court and win twenty-nine of them. The most famous was Brown v. Board of Education, decided in 1954, in which the Court declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional.
725.explanation: Marshall's long training in legal reasoning allowed him to argue repeatedly and successfully before the highest court in the land.
725.tie_back: The kural urges study of the proper method of reasoning so that one can answer in an assembly without fear, and Marshall's disciplined legal training made him a fearless advocate before the Supreme Court.
725._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for trained reasoning producing confident advocacy, but the sources do not describe his courtroom exchanges in detail, so the link to fearless replies is general.

726.event_title: Copernicus withholds On the Revolutions until the end of his life
726.event: Nicolaus Copernicus privately circulated an outline of his sun-centred system around 1514, but his full work, De revolutionibus, with its mathematical proofs, was not published until 1543, the year of his death. Publication came only after his supporter Georg Joachim Rheticus had printed a summary in 1540 or 1541 and then arranged the printing of the full book. In his dedication to Pope Paul III, Copernicus anticipated many of the objections his ideas would raise.
726.explanation: Scholars have taken the long delay as a sign that Copernicus was well aware of the furore his work might cause among the learned.
726.tie_back: The kural asks what use books are to one who fears an assembly of sharp minds, and for decades Copernicus's knowledge sat largely unused because he hesitated to set it before the learned.
726._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit, though his reasons for delay are inferred by historians from the preface rather than stated as plain fear, and his work was eventually published.

727.event_title: Henry Cavendish's electrical discoveries stay unpublished for a century
727.event: Henry Cavendish published an early version of his theory of electricity in 1771, but although he continued to work on the subject he published nothing more on it. His manuscripts, recording many careful experiments, remained with his family for about a hundred years. James Clerk Maxwell acquired them in 1874 and published an edition in 1879, showing that Cavendish had anticipated results later credited to others.
727.explanation: Results that could have advanced the science of electricity in Cavendish's lifetime lay hidden, so that others received the credit for rediscovering them.
727.tie_back: The kural compares the learning of one who will not use it before the assembly to a gleaming sword in a hand that never strikes, and Cavendish's unpublished electrical work is a vivid case of fine learning left unused.
727._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of valuable knowledge kept from others; the sources consulted do not state that fear of the scientific community was his reason.

728.event_title: Josiah Willard Gibbs's great work on thermodynamics goes long unappreciated
728.event: Between 1876 and 1878 Josiah Willard Gibbs of Yale published On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances, a long paper that introduced the phase rule and is now seen as a landmark of physical chemistry. It appeared in the Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences in a dense, highly mathematical form that most contemporaries found very hard to follow. Its value was recognised only gradually, helped by James Clerk Maxwell and by later translations into German in 1892 and French in 1899.
728.explanation: Gibbs's ideas were among the most important of his century, yet because they were not put in a form most scientists could grasp, years passed before they had their full effect.
728.tie_back: The kural warns that however much a person has learned, it bears no fruit if it is not set persuasively before the assembly, and the slow reception of Gibbs's treatise shows that cost.
728._accuracy_note: Partial fit: Gibbs did publish and was admired by a few, and his difficulty lay in style rather than any fear of speaking, though the delay in his influence matches the kural's warning.

729.event_title: Gauss keeps his ideas on non-Euclidean geometry private
729.event: Carl Friedrich Gauss, already one of the leading mathematicians of his age, privately discussed the possibility of a non-Euclidean geometry with friends from the early 1800s. He told his correspondent Schumacher that he believed his reputation would suffer if he admitted his belief in such a geometry in public, and he did not publish a single paper on the subject. Nikolai Lobachevsky and Janos Bolyai published their own non-Euclidean geometries first.
729.explanation: One of the greatest mathematicians of all time held back a revolutionary idea out of concern for how his peers would react, leaving the credit to others.
729.tie_back: The kural says that those who have learned and understood yet shrink from the assembly rank below even the unlearned, and Gauss's silence on non-Euclidean geometry is a well-documented case of learning withheld for fear of public reaction.
729._accuracy_note: Fits the idea of the learned dreading the assembly, though calling Gauss lower than the unlearned would be unfair, so the kural's harsh ranking is not matched.

730.event_title: Fermat's marginal note and his unpublished mathematics
730.event: Pierre de Fermat, a lawyer and councillor in Toulouse, wrote in the margin of his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica that he had found a remarkable proof of what became known as Fermat's Last Theorem, but that the margin was too small to contain it. Attempts to have his work published during his lifetime failed largely because he never wanted to put it into polished form. His marginal notes became known only after his son Samuel published them in an edition of the Arithmetica in 1670, and the theorem was not proved until the 1990s.
730.explanation: Fermat's methods and proofs, which he rarely set out in full for others, were largely lost to his contemporaries, and mathematicians spent centuries trying to recover what he claimed to know.
730.tie_back: The kural says that those who cannot pass on what they have learned so that it reaches others are like the dead though alive, and Fermat's unshared proofs left his contemporaries with little more than tantalising claims.
730._accuracy_note: Fits the failure to pass on learning, but Fermat's reluctance came from temperament and lack of interest in publishing rather than documented fear of an assembly.
